statement: Readiness signals may only convert a planned moderate/high-intensity session to an easy session (or rest). They must never add load or increase intensity.
appliesTo: All runners with a planned intensity session

statement: Intensity sessions skipped or downgraded because of a readiness flag are not rescheduled or made up. Guided arms did about 25% fewer hard sessions with similar or better outcomes.

Compute an individual morning/nocturnal HRV baseline (ln-transformed RMSSD or equivalent) as a rolling mean and SD. Flag a day when HRV is below mean minus 1 SD or falling for 2 consecutive days. Baseline method must be configurable and labelled as an unresolved default; do not flag before enough valid readings exist.
value: 10-day rolling mean minus 1 SD; or decline for 2 days; minimum 10 valid readings before flagging

statement: Use a short daily subjective wellness rating (fatigue, sleep quality, soreness, mood, stress) as the primary readiness input; HRV and resting HR are secondary corroborating signals.
Do not change the plan on a single night of one objective marker. Require either subjective corroboration or persistence of the same flag. The numeric persistence value is a conservative default.
value: 2 consecutive flagged days, or 1 flagged day plus a poor subjective score

statement: Never label a user as overreached or overtrained from HRV, resting HR or HR recovery. Rising resting RMSSD and post-exercise HRR occur in both positive adaptation and overreaching. Pair HRV with a workload-response measure (for example pace at a given HR) before suggesting negative adaptation.

When unexplained fatigue, performance decline or mood disturbance persists, suggest a deload and advise seeing a clinician, with a checklist (energy intake, iron, illness, sleep). The sources give no duration threshold; the default is a safety convention.
Resting HR is a corroborating signal only, never a stand-alone prescription trigger: it did not differ between guided and predefined training, and a falling trend occurs with normal adaptation.

Store device model with each HRV reading and apply a device-specific noise floor. Use multi-night rolling averages (not single nights) for flags, and treat HRV flags from lower-accuracy devices as low-confidence. The 10% floor is derived from MAPE values in a 13-person study.
value: 10 (devices with HRV MAPE above about 8%: Whoop, Garmin, Polar); 6 (Oura Gen 4 class); rolling average of 7 nights

statement: Treat sleep as a risk modifier: when average sleep over several nights is below about 7 h, or below the user's own stated need, show a warning and offer an intensity reduction. Never cut volume automatically, and do not penalise a single short night. The multi-night window is a default.
value: 7-night average below 7 h or below personal sleep need

statement: Use the sleep-injury association as explanatory copy only. The evidence comes from adolescents; do not apply an 8 h cut-off to adults or drive load cuts from it.

A logged illness symptom flag suspends intensity sessions. Do not infer illness from HRV or resting HR alone. Expect about a week of symptoms (mean 7.1 days). On return, run easy before any intensity, with a conservative engine convention of 1 symptom-free day before easy running and 3 easy days before intensity; this protocol is not from any source.
value: suspend intensity while symptomatic; 1 symptom-free day then easy; 3 easy days before intensity

statement: Keep pace/HR-based zones as the intensity anchor and intensity-distribution source; use HRV only as a modifier. HRV prescription showed no between-group advantage over HR or race-pace prescription at equal load.
Store sex and training level as readiness inputs, but do not hard-code sex-specific HRV thresholds. Women are under-represented and the subgroup findings are moderator-based.
appliesTo: All runners, especially women and recreational runners
